govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pre-Assassinati: A letter written in January 1964 to Toni Strassman of New York concerns poultry. The writer discusses laying chickens. The letter also mentions a gift of geese and rare ducks made to President Nkrumah of Ghana. The author's name cannot be recovered. Geese gifts to African leaders were one man's unusual diplomacy in those years, and this letter belongs to that correspondence: part farm business, part goodwill by waterfowl.
podcast-tuckercarlson-Xin0OC5e66A:
Lawyer Stefan Passantino talks with Tucker Carlson about the January 6 committee. Passantino represented witnesses who gave testimony to the panel. He says the process crossed lines that lawyers should respect.

He describes how he came to doubt the hearings as they unfolded. He accuses Liz Cheney of leading an effort to punish lawyers for Trump. Carlson asks how legal help became a political target. The episode presents a defense-side view of the probe, its methods, and the cost for lawyers who took unpopular clients. The story is told in close detail, step by step.
uslaw-usc-t1-s106a:
Section 106a of Title 1 governs the promulgation of laws, the step that puts a new law into official custody. When a bill, order, resolution, or vote of the two Houses becomes a law, it must be received by the Archivist of the United States. That holds whether the President approved it or let it take effect without return.

A veto override follows a different path. If the President returns a measure with objections, and two-thirds of both Houses pass it again, it becomes law on that vote. The original then comes to the Archivist from the presiding officer of the House where it was last approved. The Archivist must carefully preserve the originals. The section sits in Chapter 2 of Title 1, on the formalities of enactment. The hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1316a:
Section 1316a of Title 2 of the United States Code extends certain federal hiring rights to legislative branch staff. The terms covered employee and Board carry the meanings given in the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995. The rights and protections of named Title 5 provisions apply to covered employees. Those provisions cover veterans' preference and related hiring rules, as listed in the text.

The remedy for a breach matches the remedy that would fit under Title 5 for a breach of the matching provision. The steps for weighing a claimed breach are the same as those under the named section of the Accountability Act. The section thus borrows the executive branch's hiring protections for congressional staff.
uslaw-usc-t2-s166a:
Section 166a of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with access to research reports. The reports are those of the Congressional Research Service at the Library. A term in the section is CRS product, set out first in the text. It means any final writ work of the Service with research in it.

The work may be in any format, the text says at that point. It must be free for general congressional use on the Service's intranet. A second term, CRS Report, is then set in its own part. It takes in updates to past writ products of the Service. Named report kinds are listed as in the class at that spot. Closed products made for a single request are kept out of the class.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1816a:
Section 1816a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers design build contracts for the Architect of the Capitol. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on that architect's powers and duties. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It lets one office combine design and building in a single contract.

Despite any other provision of law, the Architect may use a two phase selection process for such contracts. That process is the one authorized in Title 41 for federal building work. It applies to contracts for the design and construction of a public building, facility, or work. The rule gives the Capitol's building office a modern procurement tool.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1966a:
Section 1966a of Title 2 of the United States Code provides protection for former Speakers of the House of Representatives. It sits in Chapter 29 of Title 2, on the Capitol Police, current through Public Law 119-134. The guard is time-limited and rests on a threat check.

The Capitol Police must carry out a threat assessment for each former Speaker. If the check warrants it, the former Speaker receives a Capitol Police protective detail for not more than one year from the day of leaving office. A former Speaker may turn the detail down at any time. At the end of the year, the police carry out a fresh threat assessment. The detail may then be extended past the first year, with the former Speaker's agreement, if facts or conditions such as violent threats warrant it.
uslaw-usc-t2-s276a: Section 276a of Title 2 of the United States Code sits in the chapter on the Office of Legislative Counsel, in the part for the Senate. It is a short spending clause for that office. With the approval of the President Pro Tempore of the Senate, the Legislative Counsel may make such expenditures as are needed. The spending must be necessary or fit for the working of the office. The clause gates the authority with one officer's approval.
